court: The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section)

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found the complaint under Article 2 was not manifestly ill-founded and admissible under Article 35 § 3.

holdings.text: Holds that there has been a violation of Article 2 of the Convention
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court concluded the investigation was inadequate and the State failed to provide a plausible explanation for the death, thus violating Article 2.

holdings.text: Holds that there is no need to examine separately the complaints under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention
holdings.reasoning_summary: Given the violation of Article 2, the Court deemed it unnecessary to examine separately the complaints under Articles 6 and 13.

holdings.text: Holds that the respondent State is to pay, within three months from the date on which the judgment becomes final in accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, the following amounts, to be converted into Turkish liras at the rate applicable at the date of settlement: (i) to the first applicant, Mrs Fadik Beker, EUR 16,500 in respect of pecuniary damage and EUR 20,000 in respect of non-pecuniary damage, plus any tax that may be chargeable; (ii) to each of the other three applicants, EUR 5,000 plus any tax that may be chargeable, in respect of non-pecuniary damage; and (iii) to the four applicants jointly, EUR 2,000 in respect of costs and expenses, plus any tax that may be chargeable to them; and that from the expiry of the above-mentioned three months until settlement simple interest shall be payable on the above amounts at a rate equal to the marginal lending rate of the European Central Bank during the default period plus three percentage points
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court awarded pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages and costs to the applicants based on the violation of Article 2 and established causal link to pecuniary loss.

holdings.text: Dismisses the remainder of the applicants’ claim for just satisfaction.
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court dismissed any other claims for just satisfaction beyond those awarded.

anchor.surface_text: ...according to the Court’s established case-law, States bear the burden of providing plausible explanations for injuries and deaths occurred in custody, failing which a clear issue arises under Article 3 or 2 of the Convention (see, respectively, Selmouni v. France [GC], no. 25803/94, § 87, ECHR 1999‑V; Salman v. Turkey [GC], no. 21986/93, § 99, ECHR 2000-VII). The underlying reason for this is that persons in custody are in a vulnerable position and that the authorities are under a duty to protect them.

precedents.cited_proposition: States bear the burden of providing plausible explanations for injuries and deaths occurred in custody under Article 2 or 3
precedents.cited_holding: States must provide plausible explanations for deaths in custody to avoid violation of Articles 2 or 3

anchor.surface_text: Since the adoption of the judgment in the case of Akkum and Others v. Turkey, the above-mentioned obligation has been held to cover injuries or deaths which occurred, not only in custody, but also in areas within the exclusive control of the authorities of the State because, in both situations, the events in issue lie wholly, or in large part, within the exclusive knowledge of the authorities (no. 21894/93, § 211, ECHR 2005‑II (extracts); see also Yasin Ateş v. Turkey, no. 30949/96, § 94, 31 May 2005).
